Typhoid (also called typhoid fever) is a serious, potentially life-threatening infectious disease caused by a specific bacterium called Salmonella Typhi. It primarily affects the intestines and can spread to the bloodstream and other organs if not treated in time.

The word is used both as a standalone noun ("he was diagnosed with typhoid") and as a shorthand for the full phrase "typhoid fever."
What Causes It?

A tiny, single-celled organism called Salmonella Typhi is entirely responsible. This is a bacterium — a living microorganism — and it is different from the Salmonella that causes ordinary food poisoning. Salmonella Typhi is far more dangerous and behaves very differently in the body. It doesn't just irritate the gut; it invades the bloodstream and travels through the entire body.
How Does It Spread?

Typhoid spreads through what scientists call the fecal-oral route. This means:

  1. An infected person passes the bacteria in their stool (and sometimes urine).
  2. If proper sanitation is absent, that bacteria contaminates water or food.
  3. Another person consumes that contaminated water or food.
  4. The bacteria enter their body and the infection begins.

The most common sources of infection are:

  • Contaminated drinking water — the most significant route worldwide.
  • Food handled by infected people who didn't wash their hands properly.
  • Raw fruits and vegetables washed or grown using contaminated water.
  • Street food in regions where sanitation is poor.

You cannot catch typhoid simply by being near an infected person or breathing the same air. It requires ingestion — something contaminated must enter your mouth.
What Happens Inside the Body?

Once Salmonella Typhi enters the small intestine, it doesn't stay there. It passes through the intestinal wall, enters the lymph nodes, and then moves into the bloodstream — a process called bacteraemia. From there, it spreads to the liver, spleen, bone marrow, and gallbladder. The gallbladder is particularly important because the bacteria can live there for a long time, which is relevant to the idea of "carriers" (explained below).

The body recognises the invasion and mounts an immune response, but Salmonella Typhi has clever mechanisms to survive inside white blood cells, making it harder to eliminate quickly.
Symptoms: What It Feels Like

Typhoid doesn't strike all at once. It follows a gradual pattern, typically unfolding over weeks if untreated.

The incubation period (time from infection to first symptoms) is usually 1 to 3 weeks, though it can range from 6 days to 30 days depending on the dose of bacteria consumed and the person's immunity.

Week 1:

  • A fever that climbs slowly and steadily, eventually reaching 39–40°C (102–104°F).
  • Headache, fatigue, and a general feeling of being unwell.
  • Dry cough.
  • Stomach pain and loss of appetite.

Week 2:

  • The fever remains high and sustained (unlike flu, which tends to fluctuate more).
  • In some patients, small pink or rose-coloured spots called "rose spots" appear on the abdomen and chest. These are faint, slightly raised rashes and are considered a classic sign of typhoid, though they appear in only a minority of patients.
  • Either diarrhoea or constipation, depending on the person. This varies, which sometimes makes diagnosis tricky.
  • An enlarged spleen or liver may be felt.
  • Mental dullness or confusion in some cases — giving the illness a heavy, almost stuporous quality, which is reflected in the word's history.

Week 3 (if untreated):

  • The illness can worsen severely.
  • Serious complications such as intestinal bleeding or perforation (a hole forming in the intestinal wall) can occur.
  • Without treatment, the death rate historically ranged from 10–30%. With modern antibiotics, it drops to below 1%.

Recovery (Week 4 onwards):

  • In survivors without complications, the fever gradually falls and the person recovers, but weakness and fatigue can persist for weeks.
Who Is Most at Risk?

Typhoid is closely linked to poor sanitation and limited access to clean drinking water. It is most common in:

  • South Asia — India, Pakistan, Bangladesh, and Nepal have among the highest rates globally.
  • Southeast Asia — particularly Indonesia, Vietnam, and the Philippines.
  • Sub-Saharan Africa and parts of Latin America.

Children between 5 and 15 years of age are disproportionately affected, though people of all ages can get it.

Travellers from countries with good sanitation who visit high-risk areas are also vulnerable, because they haven't built up any immunity and may be less cautious about food and water.
Diagnosis

A doctor who suspects typhoid will typically order:

  • Blood culture — the most definitive test, especially in the first week. Blood is drawn and checked for the presence of Salmonella Typhi.
  • Bone marrow culture — the most accurate test, but rarely done because it's invasive.
  • Widal test — an older blood test that looks for antibodies; widely used but not very reliable.
  • Stool and urine cultures — useful in later stages.
Treatment

Typhoid is treated with antibiotics. Before antibiotics were discovered, typhoid was a major killer. The antibiotics commonly used today include:

  • Fluoroquinolones (like ciprofloxacin) — once the go-to treatment.
  • Third-generation cephalosporins (like ceftriaxone) — now widely used because of growing resistance to fluoroquinolones.
  • Azithromycin — commonly recommended for uncomplicated typhoid, especially for travellers.

Antibiotic resistance is a serious and growing problem. Strains of Salmonella Typhi resistant to multiple antibiotics — including extensively drug-resistant (XDR) typhoid — have emerged and spread, particularly from Pakistan. This makes treatment harder and is a major global health concern.

Alongside antibiotics, treatment includes rest, fluids to prevent dehydration, and careful nutrition. In cases of intestinal perforation, surgery may be required.
Prevention

Typhoid is entirely preventable. The key measures are:

1. Vaccines:
Two vaccines are available:

  • Ty21a — a live oral vaccine taken as capsules (3–4 doses on alternate days). It offers protection for about 5–7 years.
  • Vi polysaccharide vaccine (ViCPS) — a single injection that provides protection for about 2–3 years.
  • Typhoid conjugate vaccine (TCV) — a newer, more effective injectable vaccine, especially recommended for children, as it provides longer-lasting immunity and can be given from 6 months of age. This is now being introduced in vaccination programmes in high-burden countries.

Importantly, no vaccine is 100% effective, and protection is not lifelong — boosters are needed. Vaccines are strongly recommended for travellers to endemic regions.

2. Safe water and food:

  • Drink only boiled, bottled, or chemically treated water.
  • Avoid ice in drinks in areas where water safety is uncertain.
  • Eat food that is thoroughly cooked and served hot.
  • Avoid raw vegetables and salads in endemic areas.
  • Peel fruits yourself before eating.

3. Hand hygiene:

  • Thorough handwashing with soap and water after using the toilet and before handling food is critical — both at the individual level and, more importantly, as a system-wide public health measure.

4. Improved sanitation infrastructure:
On a societal level, the most powerful long-term prevention is clean water supply, proper sewage disposal, and adequate sanitation — the same measures that largely eliminated typhoid from wealthy countries in the 20th century.
Typhoid Carriers: A Critical Concept

One of the most important and fascinating aspects of typhoid is the existence of chronic carriers. After recovering from typhoid, a small percentage of people (about 1–5%) continue to harbour Salmonella Typhi in their gallbladder. The bacteria live there without causing the person any harm or noticeable symptoms — but are silently shed in their stool, making the person a silent, ongoing source of infection for others.

The most famous example in history is Mary Mallon, known as Typhoid Mary, an Irish-American cook in New York City in the early 1900s. She infected dozens of people across multiple households over years, while feeling perfectly healthy herself. She was eventually forcibly quarantined for the rest of her life after refusing to stop working as a cook.

Chronic carriers are often identified through contact tracing after an outbreak. Treatment (long-course antibiotics, sometimes combined with removal of the gallbladder) can eliminate the carrier state.
Typhoid vs. Paratyphoid

A closely related illness, paratyphoid fever, is caused by Salmonella Paratyphi A, B, or C. It spreads in the same way and causes very similar symptoms, but is generally milder and less likely to be fatal. Together, typhoid fever and paratyphoid fever are collectively called enteric fever (from enteric, meaning "relating to the intestines"). When doctors use the term "enteric fever," they are referring to both.
Typhoid in History

Before the 20th century, typhoid was one of the deadliest infectious diseases in the world. It swept through armies, crowded cities, and refugee camps. It killed several historical figures, including Prince Albert (Queen Victoria's husband) and possibly Abraham Lincoln's son Willie. Entire military campaigns were hampered more by typhoid than by enemy fire.

The disease began to be controlled through two major developments: clean water supply systems and sewage treatment (starting in the late 19th century) and the introduction of effective antibiotics (mid-20th century). Countries that invested in sanitation infrastructure saw typhoid rates collapse, even before widespread vaccination. This is why typhoid is today rare in wealthy, developed nations but remains a significant killer in lower-income countries — with an estimated 9 to 11 million cases and over 100,000 deaths per year globally.
Complications (If Left Untreated)

The most dangerous complication of typhoid is intestinal perforation — a hole that forms in the wall of the small intestine, usually in the third week of illness. This allows the contents of the intestine to spill into the abdominal cavity, causing peritonitis (severe abdominal infection), which can be rapidly fatal without surgery.

Other complications include:

  • Internal intestinal bleeding
  • Hepatitis (liver inflammation)
  • Myocarditis (inflammation of the heart muscle)
  • Encephalitis (brain inflammation) — causing confusion, delirium, seizures
  • Pneumonia
  • Meningitis (rarely)
In Summary

AspectKey Point

To put it plainly: typhoid is a severe bacterial infection of the intestines and bloodstream caused by Salmonella Typhi, spread through contaminated food and water in areas with poor sanitation. It causes a prolonged, sustained fever along with abdominal symptoms and can be fatal if untreated. It is treated with antibiotics, prevented through vaccines and clean water, and is a major ongoing public health challenge in South Asia and Africa.
